hints: Look at the shape and shading of each amino acid in order from the N terminal end to the C terminal end, and mark every place where a light oval (non-polar) sits next to any other shape.
Remember a cut is made only at a non-polar to polar junction in either direction, then use cuts + 1 to get total fragments and look for single amino acids trapped between two cuts.
walkthrough:
**Sort the shapes into two groups**

Think like a teacher with a highlighter. Light ovals are non-polar. All other shapes are polar of some kind: dark squares are polar basic, white hexagons are polar acidic, grey hexagons are polar.

Rule for this enzyme:
$$cut \ only \ if \ non\text{-}polar \ next \ to \ polar$$

**Walk the chain and mark every cut**

Start at the N terminal Lys and move along the whole polypeptide to the C terminal Glu. Put a mark between neighbours where one is a light oval and the other is any polar shape.

You will find 16 such junctions, for example Thr to Ala, Ala to Lys, Lys to Phe, Phe to Glu, and so on around the long chain.

**Convert cuts to total fragments**

Each hydrolysis breaks one peptide bond, so one long chain cut in 16 places gives:
$$total \ fragments = cuts + 1 = 16 + 1 = 17$$

**Spot the single amino acids**

A single amino acid forms when both its left bond and its right bond are cut. Scanning the 16 cuts shows this happens 4 times: Lys, Phe, Met and Leu are each isolated.

So singles = 4, and the rest are small peptides:
$$small \ peptides = 17 - 4 = 13$$

options.A: Too low. It misses most of the 16 non-polar to polar junctions along the long chain.
options.B: Still too low. It counts only about half the correct cuts and misses singles like Phe, Met and Leu.
options.C: Close but undercounts by one single and one peptide, often by missing the Lys to Phe to Glu double cut at the N end.
options.D: Correct. 16 cuts give 17 fragments, made up of 4 single amino acids and 13 small peptides.
